comment: Each ratio is how many times slower than the same mapping written by hand, measured in the
same run. Times are not compared: a shared runner is slow and erratic in ways that move the
hand-written baseline too, so the ratio survives what the nanoseconds do not.
The tolerance is deliberately loose to begin with. A check that cries wolf gets ignored, and
there is no data yet on how much these move between runners. What it has to catch is a
regression of the size that actually happens: switching off the inlining puts the collection
back from 1.79x to 2.65x, and losing the plan cache costs a third of a flat map. Both are far
outside 25 per cent. Tighten this once a few runs have shown what the real spread is.
A scenario may set its own tolerance, for when one of them turns out to be steadier or
noisier than the rest. Nested has one: at 25 per cent a run with the inlining switched off
measured 2.80x and passed, which is not much of a guard, so it is held tighter. Enums by
value has one the other way: five casts written by hand take four nanoseconds, and a ratio
over a floor that small moves about ten per cent between runs on this machine. The record
through its constructor has one for the same reason and a sharper demonstration of it: on
unchanged code the short job reported 4.91x and a full-length run of the same scenario
reported 2.99x. A hand-written floor of five nanoseconds and three iterations do not resolve
each other.
Raising a number here is how a change that is meant to cost something gets agreed. Do it in
the same pull request, never afterwards.
Not every scenario belongs here. The projection needs a database and its ratio is mostly
Entity Framework's. The concurrent one measures contention, and how much shows up depends on
the core count of whatever runner picked up the job.
Both halves of the enum scenario are held. Neither was worth holding before: by name cost
25x and by value 15x, and pinning those would have protected nothing. What a regression in
either would mean now is that the work went back to being done per call instead of once,
while the plan was compiled.
By name then earned a tolerance of its own, the third scenario to do so and for the reason
the other two did. CI reported 6.07x against 4.56x on a change that touches nothing it
runs: the only run-time edit in that pull request is a branch taken while a plan is
compiled, and only for a pair whose destination is an enum, which this scenario's is not.
Six short runs were taken to check it anyway — 4.14x, 4.44x and 3.45x on the branch, 3.65x,
4.09x and 3.70x on main. The two sets overlap and each spans about a whole point. The
hand-written floor is five switch statements, seven to eleven nanoseconds, and it moved
seventeen per cent between consecutive runs over code that had not changed.
Mapperion_Bound is MapperFor's number, and it is held because it is the one arrangement
measured under Mapster. A regression there would mean the dispatch or the plan lookup
crept back into the per-object path, which is the whole of what it removes.
